q: You are showing a new crew member the sextant before her first sun sight on the ARC. What moves when she turns the micrometer drum?
a: The index arm, with the index mirror on it
o: The horizon mirror on the frame
The telescope in its collar
The shade glasses in front of the mirrors
why: The drum drives the index arm along the arc and the index mirror turns with it; the horizon mirror and telescope are fixed to the frame.

q: You read your micrometer sextant after a sun sight. What is Hs?
why: Degrees from the arc (the last whole degree passed, 41°), minutes from the drum (58′), tenths from the vernier (0.6′).

fig.title: Your sextant after the sight
lines: Index mark on the arc: just past 41°

q: You are about to bring the Sun down to the horizon. What do you swing in first?
a: Index shades, enough to dim the Sun's image
o: Horizon shades only — the Sun is seen direct
No shades — the telescope cuts the glare
One light horizon shade, no index shade
why: The Sun's image comes via the index mirror: dim it with index shades before you look. Horizon shades only cut the glare on the sea.

fig.title: Sun sight, late morning
lines: Clear sky, the Sun very bright
Sextant set near 0°, all shades up

q: The sea is lumpy and you take the sextant out of its box for the noon sight. How do you lift it?
a: By the handle or frame — never the arc or arm
o: By the arc — the strongest part of the frame
By the index arm, with the clamp released
By the telescope — it is bolted to the frame
why: Lifting by the arc or the index arm can bend it and add an error; hold the frame or handle, and put it straight back in the box.

q: You are working up a sun sight. Which altitude do you enter the main correction table with?
a: Ha — Hs after index error and dip
o: Hs — the reading straight off the arc
Ho — the altitude after every correction
Hc — the altitude from the sight reduction
why: Hs ± IE − dip = Ha (apparent altitude); refraction and SD depend on Ha, so the main table is entered with Ha to give Ho.

fig.title: Sun LL — working
lines: Main correction: enter the table with ?

q: You bought a second-hand sextant for a Pacific crossing and want to adjust it. In what order do you remove the errors?
a: Perpendicularity, side error, then index error
o: Index error, side error, then perpendicularity
Side error, perpendicularity, then index error
Index error, perpendicularity, then side error
why: Each adjustment can upset the next: the index mirror first (perpendicularity), then the horizon mirror for side error, then index error.

q: Your crew asks why you swing the sextant from side to side as the Sun touches the horizon. What are you doing?
a: Finding the bottom of the arc — the sextant upright
o: Shaking water drops off the horizon mirror
Averaging out the boat's roll
Checking the sextant for side error
why: Rocking swings the Sun in an arc; at its lowest point the sextant is vertical. Set the lower limb to kiss the horizon there.

fig.title: Sun sight from the deck
lines: Sun's lower limb near the horizon
You swing the sextant gently left and right
The Sun's image swings in an arc

q: You are alone on watch and want the time of your sight to the second. How do you get it?
a: Start a stopwatch at the sight, then read the watch
o: Read the watch after you have read the sextant
Note the time as you go on deck to take it
Read the watch first, then take the sight
why: Start the stopwatch at the instant of the sight; at the chart table read the watch and subtract the stopwatch's run.

fig.title: Single-handed sight
lines: GPS-checked watch at the chart table
No one on deck to call 'mark'

q: You take the sight on the Sun's upper limb. How does the semi-diameter go into the correction?
a: Subtracted — the centre is below the upper limb
o: Added, as for every sun sight
Ignored — it is part of the dip
Added twice — for the whole diameter
why: The tables give the altitude of the Sun's centre: add SD to a lower-limb sight, subtract it from an upper-limb sight.

fig.title: Afternoon sun sight
lines: Low cloud hides the Sun's lower half
Upper limb sharp above the cloud
You bring the upper limb to the horizon

q: You take a sight with the plastic backup sextant. What do you do about its index error?
a: Measure it again now, just before the sight
o: Use the 2.0′ off the arc from breakfast
Ignore it — plastic sextants have none
Use the metal sextant's index error
why: A plastic frame bends with temperature, so its index error changes within hours: check it at every sight.

fig.title: Backup sextant
lines: Plastic sextant from the grab bag
Left in the sun in the cockpit for an hour
IE was 2.0′ off the arc at breakfast

q: You take your sights standing at the shrouds of a 15 m ketch. What dip do you apply?
why: Dip = 1.76 × √3.2 = 1.76 × 1.79 = 3.1′, always subtracted from Hs.

q: You check the index error on the horizon before the morning sights. What is it, and how do you apply it?
a: 3.0′ off the arc: add it
o: 3.0′ on the arc: subtract it
57.0′ off the arc: add it
3.0′ off the arc: subtract it
why: Below zero the drum reads 60′ minus the error: 60 − 57.0 = 3.0′ off the arc, and off the arc is added to Hs.

fig.title: Index error on the horizon
lines: Direct and reflected horizon in one line

q: At twilight you check the index error on a bright star. What correction do you apply to tonight's sights?
a: Subtract 2.4′
o: Add 2.4′
Subtract 1.2′
Add 4.8′
why: A reading on the arc for a zero angle means the sextant reads too high: subtract 2.4′ from every Hs.

fig.title: Index error on a star
lines: Reflected and direct star made one

q: You read the sextant after a sight of Arcturus. What is the altitude after the index error?
why: The reading is 52°14.6′; off the arc is added: 52°14.6′ + 1.4′ = 52°16.0′.

q: You are 1300 miles from St Lucia on the ARC and take this sight of the Sun. What is Ho?

fig.title: Sun LL, 20 November
lines: IE 2.0′ on the arc · eye 2.7 m (dip 2.9′)

q: Bound from Bermuda to the Azores, you catch the Sun's upper limb between clouds. What is Ho?
In mid-Atlantic you take Vega at nautical twilight. What is Ho?
why: 41°20.0′ − 1.6′ IE − 2.6′ dip − 1.1′ refraction = Ho 41°14.7′; a star has no semi-diameter.

q: You add Jupiter to your evening star fix. Which corrections take its Hs to Ho?
a: IE, dip and refraction — as for a star
o: IE, dip, refraction and the Sun's SD
IE, dip, refraction and the Moon's parallax
Dip and refraction — IE is for the Sun only
why: Jupiter is a point of light like a star: index error, dip and star refraction. Only Venus and Mars get a small additional correction.

fig.title: Dusk sights
lines: Jupiter bright in the east, Ha 33°
Almanac: no additional correction for Jupiter

q: You take the Moon in the afternoon to cross with a sun line. What is the parallax correction?
o: Subtract 49.4′
why: HP × cos Ha = 57.0′ × 0.866 = 49.4′, always added: seen from the Earth's centre the Moon stands higher.

fig.title: Moon sight
lines: Parallax in altitude = HP × cos Ha

q: You want a Moon sight just after sunset. Which limb do you bring to the horizon?
a: The lower limb — it is the lit edge
o: The upper limb — the tips of the crescent
The centre, judged by eye
Either — the semi-diameter is the same
why: Only the lit, round limb is a true edge of the Moon's disc; here it faces down, so take the lower limb and add SD.

fig.title: Evening, west sky
lines: Thin crescent Moon above the sunset
Lit edge facing down, towards the Sun

q: You take the Sun soon after sunrise because cloud is coming in. What is Ho?
Off the west coast of Barbados at 0800 you want a sun line, but the Sun is over the island. What do you do with the shoreline under it?
a: Don't use it — its dip is not the table's
o: Use it with the dip from the table
Use it and double the table's dip
Use it with no dip — land is level
why: The shoreline lies inside the sea horizon, so it dips more than the table gives; take a body over open sea instead.

fig.title: Sun sight off Barbados
lines: Coast 1.5 M away, under the Sun
Eye 2.5 m: sea horizon 3.3 M off

q: In a big Southern Ocean swell you bring the Sun down to the crest of a nearby wave. What does that do, and what do you do?
a: Hs reads low — sight from the top of a swell
o: Hs reads high — sight from the trough
No effect — the dip allows for it
Hs reads low — add the wave height to the dip
why: A crest above your eye stands higher than the true horizon, so Hs reads low; wait for the boat to lift and sight from the top.

fig.title: Southern Ocean swell, 4 m
lines: In the troughs a crest hides the horizon
The boat lifts to each swell

q: On the ARC route the horizon under the Sun is blurred by dust. What gives you a better sight?
a: Sight from lower down, with the dip for that height
o: Sight from higher up — the horizon is further off
Keep the height and add 2′ for the haze
Use the top of the haze as the horizon
why: A lower eye brings the horizon nearer and sharper in haze; use the dip for the new height of eye.

fig.title: Hazy horizon, 0700
lines: Saharan dust in the trade wind
Horizon fuzzy from the coachroof (3.5 m)

q: You take four quick sights of the rising Sun to average. Which time and Hs do you work up?
why: Mean of the times 09:42:20, mean of the altitudes 31°14.0′ — fine while the altitude changes steadily over a few minutes.

q: You plot five altitudes against time before averaging them. Which sight do you discard?
a: No. 3
o: No. 1
No. 4
No. 5
why: The Sun rises about 3′ every 30 s: No. 3 should be near 40°08.0′, not 40°11.9′ — a bad sight; average the other four.

q: You need a morning sun line in this sea. Where and how do you take the sight?
a: Wedged in the companionway, clipped on, on a crest
o: Standing on the coachroof, holding the boom
Sitting low in the cockpit, in the troughs
At the stern, eye as high as the pushpit
why: Brace yourself near the middle of the boat, hands free and clipped on, and take the sight as she lifts on a swell and the horizon clears.

fig.title: Trade-wind sight
lines: Wind 25 kn, 3 m swell on the beam
Two crew on deck, one at the helm

q: You check your sextant before the passage and see this. What is wrong, and what do you adjust?
a: Perpendicularity — the index mirror's screw
o: Side error — the horizon mirror's screw
Index error — the horizon mirror's second screw
Collimation — the telescope collar
why: If the arc and its reflection in the index mirror do not run on as one line, the index mirror is not perpendicular to the frame.

fig.title: Checking the sextant
lines: Sextant flat, arc away from you, arm at 60°
You look into the index mirror at the arc
The reflected arc steps up from the real arc

q: You check the sextant on a star and see this. What does it show, and what do you adjust?
a: Side error — the horizon mirror's side screw
o: Index error — the index mirror's screw
Perpendicularity — the index mirror's screw
Collimation — the telescope collar
why: If the reflected star passes beside, not through, the direct one, the horizon mirror is not perpendicular to the frame: side error.

fig.title: Checking on a star
lines: Index set at 0°, telescope on a star
The reflected star passes beside the real one

q: You check the telescope like this. What does the difference tell you?
a: The telescope is not parallel to the frame
o: The index mirror is not perpendicular
The horizon mirror has side error
The index error is 1.5′ on the arc
why: Collimation error: the line of sight is tilted to the frame, so large angles read too big. Adjust the collar, or keep bodies centred.

fig.title: Collimation check
lines: Two stars 100° apart brought into contact
Contact at the top, then at the bottom edge

q: You find this in the workbook. How far out is each position line?
a: 6 miles
o: 3 miles
12 miles
1.5 miles
why: The right +3.0′ became −3.0′: a 6.0′ altitude error, and 1′ of altitude is 1 M, so each line is 6 M out (away from its star).

fig.title: Last night's star fix
lines: Crew subtracted it from every Hs

q: You check the crew's working of a sun sight. What does the mistake do to the sun line?
a: 6 M too far towards the Sun
o: 6 M too far away from the Sun
3 M too far towards the Sun
3 M too far away from the Sun
why: Dip is always subtracted; adding 3.0′ makes Ho 6.0′ too large, so the intercept is 6 M too far towards.

fig.title: Sun line check
lines: Crew added the dip to Hs

q: A crew member works up this star sight. How far out is the position line?
a: 16 M too far towards the star
o: 16 M too far away from the star
8 M too far towards the star
32 M too far towards the star
why: +14.5′ − (−1.7′) = 16.2′, the Sun's SD: Ho is 16.2′ too large, so the line lies about 16 M too far towards.

fig.title: Star sight worked up
lines: Corrected with the Sun's LL table: +14.5′

q: You time a sun sight with the stopwatch. What is the UT of your sight?
why: 14:25:00 − 1 min 37.4 s = 14:23:22.6 by the watch; it is 4 s fast, so subtract: 14:23:18.6 ≈ 14:23:19 UT.

q: You measure the index error on the Sun's two limbs. What is it?
a: 0.8′ off the arc: add 0.8′
o: 0.8′ on the arc: subtract 0.8′
1.6′ off the arc: add 1.6′
1.6′ on the arc: subtract 1.6′
why: IE = (on − off) ÷ 2 = (31.6 − 33.2) ÷ 2 = −0.8′: off the arc, add. Check: (31.6 + 33.2) ÷ 4 = 16.2′, the almanac SD.

fig.title: Index error by the Sun, November

q: You take the Sun's upper limb and work it with the almanac's table. What is Ho?
You stand in the cockpit for your sights. What dip do you use?
why: Height of eye is above the sea, not the deck: 1.0 + 1.6 = 2.6 m, and dip = 1.76 × √2.6 = 2.8′.

fig.title: Where is your eye?
lines: Cockpit sole 1.0 m above the waterline
Your eye 1.6 m above the cockpit sole

q: How do you find Capella in the sextant before you can see it?
a: Preset 31° and sweep the horizon near 040°
o: Set 0°, aim at the star and bring it down
Wait until it shows, then bring it down
Preset 59° and look along 220°
why: With Hc and Zn worked out in advance, preset the altitude and look along the bearing: the star shows in the mirror while the horizon is sharp.

fig.title: Evening twilight
lines: Capella not yet visible to the eye

q: Spray came over during the noon sight. What do you do before you stow the sextant?
a: Dab the salt off, dry it, then stow it in its box
o: Leave it on the chart table to dry
Rub the mirrors hard with a paper towel
Box it as it is and clean it in port
why: Salt corrodes the mirrors and arc: dab the mirrors with lens tissue (a little fresh water), dry the frame, and keep it in its box.

fig.title: After the noon sight
lines: Spray over the cockpit during the sight
Salt drops on both mirrors and the arc

q: Cloud clears and you could take the Sun now at 5°, or wait an hour for 15°. Why is waiting better?
a: Refraction is large and uncertain near the horizon
o: Dip is larger when the Sun is low
The Sun's semi-diameter grows near the horizon
The Sun's parallax is largest when low
why: Refraction grows fast below 10° and varies with temperature and pressure, so its error is uncertain; keep sights above about 10–15°.

q: Bound for the Marquesas, you cross a sun line with this Moon sight. What is Ho?

fig.title: Moon LL, afternoon
lines: Parallax in altitude = HP × cos Ha

q: In the Indian Ocean you take the Moon by day to cross with the Sun. What is Ho?

fig.title: Moon UL, morning
lines: Only the upper limb is lit

q: You measure the index error on the Sun, then take your sight. What is Ho?

fig.title: Sun, 25 November
lines: IE on the Sun: on 31.6′, off 33.2′

q: With the lower limb in cloud, you take the setting Sun's upper limb. What is Ho?
You check the crew's sun line. How far, and which way, is their position line out?
a: 2.8 M too far towards
o: 2.8 M too far away
8.8 M too far towards
4.4 M too far away
why: IE −1.5′ instead of +1.5′ = −3.0′; dip +2.9′ instead of −2.9′ = +5.8′. Ho is 2.8′ too large: 2.8 M too far towards.

fig.title: Checking the crew's sun line
lines: IE 1.5′ off the arc — crew subtracted it

q: You plot this series against time, drop the bad sight and average the rest. What do you work up?
why: The Sun climbs about 4.6′ in 40 s, so 16:07:10 should be near 28°54′: drop it. The other four average 16:06:20, 28°48.3′.

fig.title: Five sights, 40 s apart
lines: UT and Hs; the Sun climbing steadily

q: The same sextant error is suspected in all three star sights. Where on the plotting sheet do you put your fix?
a: A — the centre, equally far from all three lines
o: B — the corner where two lines cross
C — on the line of the brightest star
D — outside the triangle, past corner B
why: A constant error moves every line the same distance towards or away; with bodies 120° apart the true fix is equidistant from all three.

q: You practise sights on the way to the Azores. When the GPS later fails, what do you do with this result?
a: Subtract 2.6′ from each Ho
o: Add 2.6′ to each Ho
Set the IE to 3.6′ off the arc
Ignore it — it is under 3′
why: A steady +2.6′ over five sights is a personal error: subtract 2.6′ from each Ho, and keep checking it while the GPS still works.

fig.title: Practice while the GPS works
lines: Five sun sights; Hc from the GPS position

q: You check the crew's Moon sight. How far out is their position line?
a: About 47 M too far away
o: About 47 M too far towards
About 58 M too far away
About 24 M too far towards
why: The Sun table leaves out the Moon's parallax: 47.4′ + 15.8′ − 15.9′ = 47.3′ too small an Ho, so about 47 M too far away.

fig.title: Moon LL worked by the crew
lines: Crew used the Sun LL table (SD 15.9′)
Parallax in altitude = HP × cos Ha

q: What do you do before the dusk star sights?
a: Remove the side error, then measure IE again
o: Use 3.5′ on the arc and ignore the side error
Zero the index error first, then side error
Average the two: use 1.5′ on the arc
why: Side error is set on the horizon mirror, which moves the index error: remove side error first, then measure IE again and apply it.

fig.title: Sextant knocked off the chart table
lines: At 0° a star passes beside its reflection

q: Your crew looks through the sextant for the first time: the horizon in one half of the field, the Sun beside it. Where does the Sun's image come from?
a: The index mirror, via the horizon mirror's silvered half
o: The horizon mirror's clear half, seen direct
The telescope's lens, without any mirror
The shade glasses, by their own reflection
why: Sunlight hits the index mirror, then the silvered half of the horizon mirror, then the telescope; the clear half shows the horizon direct.

fig.title: First look through the sextant
lines: One half of the field: the sea horizon
The other half: the Sun, dimmed by shades

q: Twilight is coming and you fit a telescope for the star sights. Which do you choose?
a: The low-power, wide-field star telescope
o: The 7× telescope, for the most magnification
The Sun telescope, with its dark filter on
The 7× telescope, a little out of focus
why: A low power (about 3×) with a wide field finds the star, holds it in a rolling boat and shows it while the horizon is still sharp.

fig.title: In the sextant box
lines: Boat rolling in the trade-wind swell

q: At night the horizon is lost in the dark but the stars are bright. A crew member suggests the old aircraft bubble sextant aboard. What is the catch at sea?
a: The boat's motion moves the bubble: errors of miles
o: None — it is more accurate than a marine sextant
It needs a larger dip than a marine sextant
It works only on the Sun, never on stars
why: A bubble sextant needs no horizon and no dip, but the yacht's roll and pitch throw the bubble about: a single sight can be many miles out.

fig.title: Night sights?
lines: Aircraft bubble sextant in a locker

q: You are stowing the gear for a three-week Atlantic crossing. Where does the sextant box live?
a: Wedged low near the middle of the boat, in a dry locker
o: In the forepeak, out of everyone's way
On the chart table, ready for the next sight
In a cockpit locker, close to where you sight
why: Low and amidships the motion is least; wedge the box so it cannot slide, and keep it dry and out of the sun.

q: In the tropics the Sun will pass about 87° high at noon. What makes this sight hard?
a: Finding the vertical — the Sun sweeps along the horizon
o: Refraction is largest near the zenith
Dip grows as the Sun climbs higher
No shade is dark enough for a high Sun
why: Near the zenith the Sun's azimuth swings fast and rocking shows no clear bottom of the arc, so it is hard to tell where the vertical meets the horizon.

q: The almanac gives Venus an additional altitude correction that Jupiter does not get. Why?
a: Venus comes close: its parallax and its phase
o: Venus has a semi-diameter like the Sun's
Venus is refracted more than a star
Venus is so bright that it dazzles the eye
why: Venus passes close to the Earth, so it has a small parallax, and its phase shifts the centre of its light: the almanac lists a small extra correction.

fig.title: Dusk sights
lines: Venus bright in the west, Ha 18°

q: Bound for Svalbard, the air is far colder than the almanac's standard. When does its temperature and pressure correction matter?
a: At low altitudes — below about 10°
o: At high altitudes — above about 60°
Only for the Moon, never for the Sun
At every altitude by the same amount
why: The extra correction scales with refraction itself: up to a minute at 5°, nothing worth applying above about 10–15°.

fig.title: Cold air, 74°N
lines: Sights planned at Ha 5° and Ha 40°

q: You move from the cockpit up onto the coachroof to see over the swell. What happens to the dip you apply?
a: It is larger — subtract more
o: It is smaller — the horizon is clearer
It is the same — dip depends on the sea
It is larger — and now it is added
why: Dip grows with height of eye (1.76 √h): the higher you stand, the lower the horizon looks, so more is subtracted.

q: You can buy one sextant for an ocean crossing and already own a plastic one. Which do you make the main instrument?
a: A metal one — its index error stays steady
o: The plastic one — light, and it never corrodes
The plastic one — it needs no adjustment
Either — both hold their errors equally
why: A metal frame keeps its shape through heat and knocks, so its errors stay put; a plastic one drifts with temperature — keep it as the backup.

q: You call 'mark!' at the instant of the sight and your crew reads the watch. What does she note first?
a: The seconds, then the minutes and hour
o: The hour, then the minutes and seconds
The minutes, then the seconds
The stopwatch, then the watch
why: The seconds change while she reads; note them first and the minutes and hour after, which will not have moved.

fig.title: Sight with a timekeeper
lines: You at the shrouds with the sextant
Crew at the chart table with the watch

q: The morning horizon is too hazy for an index check, so you use the Sun's two limbs instead. What is the index error, and which way does it go?
a: 1.9′ on the arc: subtract it
o: 1.9′ off the arc: add it
3.8′ on the arc: subtract it
1.9′ on the arc: add it

fig.title: Index error by the Sun, 15 October

q: You measure the index error on the Sun twice, a few minutes apart. Which measurement do you trust, and what is the error?
a: The first — IE 0.3′ on the arc
o: The second — IE 1.7′ on the arc
The first — IE 0.3′ off the arc
The second — IE 1.7′ off the arc
why: (on + off) ÷ 4 should be the SD: 64.4 ÷ 4 = 16.1′, good; 62.8 ÷ 4 = 15.7′, a poor contact. IE = (32.5 − 31.9) ÷ 2 = 0.3′ on.

fig.title: Index error by the Sun, 10 March

q: You step up from the cockpit onto the coachroof for the sight. What dip do you apply now?
why: Height of eye 2.4 + 0.9 = 3.3 m above the sea; dip = 1.76 × √3.3 = 1.76 × 1.82 = 3.2′.

fig.title: Height of eye
lines: Cockpit: eye 2.4 m above the sea

q: You and a crew member take the Sun's lower limb at the same moment. Whose Hs reads higher, and by how much?
a: Yours, higher by 0.8′
o: Yours, lower by 0.8′
Yours, higher by 2.6′
Neither — they read the same
why: A higher eye sees the horizon lower: dip 3.4′ at 3.7 m against 2.6′ at 2.2 m, so your Hs is 0.8′ more; after dip both give the same Ho.

q: You are crossing to the Marquesas on a 14 m catamaran in a big swell. Where do you take the morning sun sight, and with what dip?
a: The flybridge, with the dip for 4.8 m (3.9′)
o: The flybridge, with the cockpit dip (2.6′)
The cockpit, with the nearest crest as horizon
The flybridge, no dip — the horizon is clear
why: Sight where the horizon is clear and use the dip for that height: 1.76 × √4.8 = 3.9′. A nearby crest is not the horizon.

fig.title: Catamaran, 4 m swell
lines: Cockpit: eye 2.1 m, crests hide the horizon

q: Crossing the Arabian Sea in May, you take the Sun just after sunrise, before the haze thickens. What is Ho?
Cold air lies over the warm Gulf Stream and you suspect the dip is not what the table says. How do you plan the dusk star sights?
a: All four — two opposite pairs
o: A and B only — 90° apart cuts best
Only the two highest, clear of the dip
A, B and C — three are always enough
why: A dip error moves every line the same way, towards or away; in opposite pairs it cancels — the fix lies midway between each pair.

q: Off the Cape Verdes you take Venus at dusk to add to the star fix. What is Ho?
why: 22°36.4′ − 1.1′ − 2.5′ = Ha 22°32.8′; − 2.4′ refraction + 0.3′ Venus = Ho 22°30.7′. A planet takes no SD.

q: In the early afternoon you want the Moon to cross with your sun line. Which limb do you bring to the horizon, and what happens to the SD?
a: The upper limb — subtract the SD
o: The lower limb — add the SD
The upper limb — add the SD
The centre — no SD at all
why: Take the lit, round limb: with the Sun higher than the Moon it is the upper one, and an upper-limb sight takes the SD off.

fig.title: Afternoon sky
lines: The Moon's lit side faces up, to the Sun

q: Going over the crew's Moon sight at the chart table, you spot this slip with the parallax. Where does it put their Moon line?
a: About 31 M too far towards the Moon
o: About 31 M too far away from the Moon
About 58 M too far towards the Moon
About 27 M too far towards the Moon
why: Parallax in altitude = HP × cos Ha = 58.4 × 0.466 = 27.2′; adding 58.4′ makes Ho 31.2′ too large: about 31 M too far towards.

fig.title: Moon sight, crew's working
lines: Crew added the whole HP as parallax

q: A crew member took the Moon's HP and SD from the wrong day's page. How far out is her Moon line?
a: About 6 M too far away from the Moon
o: About 6 M too far towards the Moon
About 4 M too far away from the Moon
About 2 M too far away from the Moon
why: Parallax 60.1 × 0.766 = 46.0′ vs 41.8′ (4.2′) and the SD 1.5′ short: Ho 5.7′ too small, so the line is about 6 M too far away.

fig.title: Moon LL, Ha 40°00′
lines: Parallax in altitude = HP × cos Ha

q: Bound from the Caribbean to the Azores in May, you take the Sun a few minutes before it crosses your meridian. How do you plot this sight?
a: A circle of 160 M radius round the Sun's GP
o: A straight position line from an AP, as usual
A circle of 320 M radius round the Sun's GP
A circle of 160 M radius round your DR
why: At 87°20′ the circle of equal altitude is small: radius = zenith distance 2°40′ = 160 M. Plot it as a circle round the GP, not a straight line.

fig.title: Sun near the zenith, 25 May, 1512 UT

q: You plot five sun sights against time and draw the line of best fit. What Hs do you take off the line for 10:24:00 UT?
why: The line follows the steady climb (about 8.6′ a minute); at 10:24:00 it reads 33°19.3′, smoother than any single sight.

fig.title: Five sights of the rising Sun
lines: UT and Hs; the Sun climbing steadily

q: Last night's three star lines: two cross neatly, the third is far off. What most likely went wrong with the third?
a: The arc misread by a whole degree
o: The index error applied the wrong way
The dip added instead of subtracted
The drum misread by ten minutes
why: With the drum near 60′ the index sits almost on the next degree: an Hs read 1° high gives an intercept near 60′ instead of the real one.

q: Checking the sextant after your sun sight, you see that the reading you wrote down is wrong. What had that done to your sun line?
a: It was 10 M too far towards the Sun
o: It was 10 M too far away from the Sun
It was 1 M too far towards the Sun
It was 20 M too far towards the Sun
why: The true Hs is 23°32.6′, 10′ less than worked: Ho was 10′ too large, so the line was 10 M too far towards the Sun.

fig.title: Sun sight, rechecked
lines: Sextant still shows: 23° on the arc

q: The sextant slid off the cockpit seat. You check it as below. What do you do with the index error?
a: Apply 2.2′ on the arc, rechecked at each sight
o: Apply the old 0.4′ off the arc
Apply the mean, 0.9′ on the arc
Apply 2.6′ on the arc — the change
why: A small new index error is simply measured and applied; adjusting it at sea risks upsetting the side error. Recheck it before each sight.

fig.title: Checks after the knock
lines: IE now 2.2′ on the arc (was 0.4′ off)

q: Evening twilight is starting and the horizon is still sharp all round. Which star do you take first?
a: A — bright, over the eastern horizon
o: B — bright, over the western horizon
C — faint, over the eastern horizon
D — faint, over the western horizon
why: At dusk the eastern horizon fades first, and only bright stars show in the telescope yet: bright eastern stars first, western ones last.

q: Morning twilight: the horizon is just showing in the east, still dark in the west. Which star do you take first?
a: B — fainter, over the eastern horizon
o: A — brighter, over the eastern horizon
C — brighter, over the western horizon
D — fainter, over the western horizon
why: At dawn the eastern horizon sharpens first and faint stars fade first: start with faint eastern stars, finish with bright ones in the west.

q: At 0300 a bright Moon lights the sea to the south; elsewhere the horizon is lost in the dark. Which body gives you a usable sight?
a: Star P — its horizon is lit by the Moon
o: Star Q — the brightest star in the sky
Star R — farthest from the Moon's glare
Stars Q and R — the best angle of cut
why: At night a sight needs a horizon you can see, and only the sea under the Moon shows one: take the Moon and stars near its bearing.

fig.title: Night sky, 0300
lines: Star Q: Zn 060° · Star R: Zn 300°

q: Ashore before the voyage, you practise with an artificial horizon, bringing the Sun and its reflection together. What is the apparent altitude of the Sun's centre?
why: Correct the reading for IE first, then halve it: (71°36.4′ − 1.2′) ÷ 2 = 35°47.6′. No dip — the oil surface is truly level.

fig.title: Artificial horizon on the quay
lines: Tray of oil, sheltered from the wind
Sun and its reflection made to coincide

q: Bound from Cape Town to St Helena, you take Canopus at dusk and correct it with the almanac's tables. What is Ho?
why: 38°42.0′ + 0.9′ − 3.0′ = Ha 38°39.9′, inside the row; − 1.2′ = Ho 38°38.7′. A star needs no SD or parallax.

q: In the South Atlantic in January it is high summer. Which column of the almanac's Sun table do you use?
a: Oct–Mar — the column goes by the date
o: Apr–Sept — it is summer in the south
Apr–Sept — the Sun stands higher
Either — the two columns are the same
why: The columns follow the Earth–Sun distance, not the local season: in January the Sun is nearest and its SD largest, in both hemispheres.

q: The horizon is a little soft, so you measure the index error four times. What correction do you apply?
a: Add 0.4′
o: Subtract 0.4′
Add 0.5′
Add 0.8′
why: Give each reading its sign (on −, off +): (+0.6 − 0.2 + 0.8 + 0.4) ÷ 4 = +0.4′, a mean of 0.4′ off the arc, so add it.

q: You watch a new crew member take the Sun without rocking the sextant; it leans a little to one side. What does that do to her sun line?
a: Hs too large — the line too far towards
o: Hs too small — the line too far away
Hs too large — the line too far away
No effect while the limb touches
why: A tilted sextant measures down to a point of the horizon off to one side, a larger angle than the altitude: Ho too big, the line towards the Sun.

fig.title: Watching the crew's sight
lines: Lower limb set on the horizon there

q: Each time you bring Sirius down from the sky you lose it in the mirror. What is the other way to get it onto the horizon?
a: Hold the sextant upside down and bring the horizon up
o: Bring it down faster, before the boat rolls
Use more index shades so the star stands out
Defocus the telescope so the star looks bigger
why: Inverted, the sextant shows the star direct and the horizon reflected: lift the horizon to the star, turn the sextant upright and fine-tune.

fig.title: Twilight star sight
lines: Index at 0°, star in the telescope
Lost each time you swing the arm

q: In the morning the Sun climbs quickly. How do you get a clean contact of the lower limb?
a: Set the limb just below the horizon; mark as it rises to touch
o: Keep turning the drum until you see it touch
Set the limb just above and wait for it to sink
Bring it down fast and mark the first contact
why: A rising Sun brings itself to the horizon: set the limb a touch low, keep rocking, and mark the instant it just kisses the horizon.

q: With the index error removed, you look at the horizon and tilt the sextant like this. What does it show?
a: No side error
o: No index error
No perpendicularity error
No collimation error
why: If the horizon mirror leans, tilting the sextant breaks the horizon into a step. An unbroken line at any tilt means no side error.

fig.title: Checking on the horizon
lines: Set so the horizon is one line
Tilted 45° to the left, then the right
The horizon stays one unbroken line

q: In mid-Pacific the micrometer drum turns stiffly and feels gritty. What do you do?
a: Clean the rack and worm, then a drop of light oil
o: Spray water-repellent along the arc
Tighten the clamp until it runs smoothly
Leave it — the grit beds in after a while
why: Salt and grit on the rack wear the worm and spoil readings: brush them off, wipe clean, and put a trace of light oil on the worm and rack.

fig.title: Sextant after a month at sea
lines: Salt crystals on the rack teeth

q: You borrow an older vernier sextant for the passage. What does it read?
why: The arc to the last division passed, 46°40′, plus the vernier's 3′20″: 46°43′20″, and 20″ = 0.3′, so 46°43.3′.

q: Through dark index shades and a horizon shade the Sun is a crisp disc, but the horizon under it has almost vanished. What do you change?
a: Lift the horizon shade; try a lighter index shade
o: Add a darker horizon shade for contrast
Lift the index shades, keep the horizon one
Fit the star telescope to gather more light
why: Horizon shades darken the sea too: use them only against glare. Dim the Sun with index shades just enough to see both images clearly.

fig.title: Sun sight, late afternoon
lines: Index shades: the two darkest in
Horizon under the Sun: barely visible

q: On a catamaran bound for Tahiti, you measure the index error on the Sun, then take the sight from the flybridge. What is Ho?

fig.title: Sun, 5 March, flybridge
lines: IE by the Sun: on 33.6′, off 31.2′

q: Bound for Greenland through the Denmark Strait, you take Mars low in the twilight. What is Ho?
Off the Galápagos a crew member works up this Moon sight to cross with the morning sun line. What should Ho be?
why: Upper limb: the SD is subtracted. 33°05.0′ − 1.5′ + 51.1′ − 16.6′ = Ho 33°38.0′; the crew's line was 33 M too far towards the Moon.

fig.title: Moon UL, the crew's working
lines: Only the upper limb is lit

q: At dawn you take six sights of a setting star, plot them against time and fit a line. What Hs do you take off the line for 06:48:00 UT?
why: The star drops about 8.8′ a minute; 06:47:19 sits 6′ off the line — drop it. The line through the other five reads 27°35.6′ at 06:48:00.

fig.title: Six sights of a setting star
lines: UT and Hs; the star dropping steadily

q: On 18 June, some minutes before local noon near the Tropic of Cancer, you work up this sight of a very high Sun. What radius do you draw round the Sun's GP?
why: 86°50.4′ − 0.4′ − 2.9′ + 15.7′ = Ho 87°02.8′; zenith distance 90° − Ho = 2°57.2′ = 177′, so a 177 M circle round the GP.

q: You check the crew's star sight against the sextant, still untouched since the sight. What intercept should they plot?
a: 4.6 M towards
o: 64.6 M towards
4.6 M away
55.4 M away
why: The index is short of 42°, so Hs is 41°57.3′: + 0.8′ − 2.8′ − 1.1′ = Ho 41°54.2′; minus Hc 41°49.6′ = 4.6 M towards.

q: A breaking wave threw the open sextant box across the saloon. Star sights are due soon. Which instrument do you use?
a: The plastic backup, its IE checked at each sight
o: The metal one, with the mean IE of 6.5′ on
The metal one, after adjusting its index mirror
Both, and average the two sextants' altitudes
why: An IE that wanders and a loose arm mean damage the mirror screws can't fix: use the steady backup tonight and get the metal sextant repaired.

fig.title: After the fall
lines: Metal sextant: IE 5.8′ to 7.2′ on, unsteady
Its index arm wobbles on the arc
Plastic backup: IE 2.0′ off, steady 3 times

q: Early in the dusk the sky is still bright. Which three stars do you take for the fix?
a: A, E and D
o: A, B and D
A, C and D
B, C and E
why: Bright enough for the telescope (A, E, D), between 15° and 70° high (not C at 72°), and about 120° apart in bearing: A 050°, E 180°, D 290°.

fig.title: Dusk: magnitude, Zn, Hc
lines: Telescope shows mag 1.0 or brighter now

q: You and a crew member take the Sun's lower limb at the same moment, each with your own sextant. After IE and dip, how far apart are your altitudes?
With the dip in doubt over the Gulf Stream, you take two stars on opposite bearings from the same AP. What do the intercepts tell you?
a: Ho 3.0′ too high; 1.2 M towards 010°
o: Ho 3.0′ too low; 1.2 M towards 010°
Ho 1.2′ too high; 3.0 M towards 010°
Ho 3.0′ too high; 1.2 M towards 190°
why: A common error e adds to both: e = (4.2 + 1.8) ÷ 2 = 3.0′ too high; the true position is (4.2 − 1.8) ÷ 2 = 1.2 M from the AP towards 010°.
